extracted.intended_audience: professional and amateur mathematicians; readers of The Mathematician (mid-19th century)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of short 19th‑century mathematical notes: geometry (surfaces/conics), analytic results (log/antilog computation and tables), and methods for reducing integrals. Contains theorems, proofs, algorithms and worked examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables I–IV: construction and roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables required for the logarithm/antilogarithm methods: Table I — modulus M and its multiples; Table II — log 10 and multiples; Table III — Napierian and common logarithms of listed numbers; Table IV — logarithms of reciprocals (constructed by a prescribed series/formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that Table I gives M and multiples; Table II gives log10 multiples; Table III contains base Napierian and common logs of key integers; Table IV contains logs of reciprocals constructed by formula (a) using coefficients A, B, C... and shifting initial figures to obtain other rows. Emphasises computing a small core of coefficients (A,B,C,...) for one representative and obtaining others by shifting/adding to avoid recomputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm: compute log(N) to p decimal places
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure to compute either Napierian or common logarithm of any number N to p decimals: reduce N to a number between 1 and 2 (by moving decimal point and dividing by a convenient digit b), write 1 + n, obtain successive one-digit quotients r1, r2, … by dividing remainders by preceding 1+ri, and use the logarithmic product expansion to assemble log(1+n) from the −log(1−ri) contributions plus adjustments for log10 and log(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: (1) scale N so integral part becomes 1 (choose b), denote decimal part n; (2) perform successive single‑digit quotient divisions to produce r1..rm and remainder nm with at least p leading zeros; (3) use formula log(1+n) = sum_i −log(1−ri) + small remainder approximated by A·n_m (series truncation); (4) combine ±m·log10 + log b + log(1+n) to get final logN. Examples provided (Napierian of 665.8 and common log of 0.00273944) show tabulation of the −log(1−ri) contributions and assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm: compute antilogarithm (inverse) to p decimal places
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure to find the number whose log is given (antilogarithm): adjust the given logarithm by subtracting/adding multiples of log10 and the log of the greatest digit b so the remainder (−n) lies in the table range, then iteratively subtract nearest table entries log(1/(1−r)) to obtain r0, r1, … and reconstruct the antilog as 10^e × product (1 − r0)(1 − r1) … (with appropriate modulus for Napierian/common).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: (1) reduce given log by multiples of log10 and add log(b) so −n is negative and small; (2) find nearest entries in Table IV for log(1/(1−r)) to extract r0,r1,... until precision reached; (3) form product P = (1−r0)(1−r1)… and compute Antilog = 10^e · Q where Q = 1/P or as given by the derived formula; examples demonstrate reconstruction and decimal-point adjustment. Tables II–IV are used repeatedly to look up contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of modulus M and relation between Napierian and common systems
rubrics_metrics.description: The Napierian (natural) and common (base-10) systems are related via a modulus M (numerical constant M = 0.4342944819032518... or its negative in the text); common logs are obtained by multiplying Napierian logs by M and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives numerical value of M and shows how multiples of log10 and multiples of M in Table I are used to convert between systems; instructs computing Napierian logs first (A=1) then converting to common logs by multiplication by M, though an alternate direct computation for common logs is also described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property: general (non)coincidence of conjugate diameters for surfaces through eight points
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement and reasoning that, for two general quadric surfaces passing through the same eight points in space, the conjugate diameters to sections parallel to a given plane will not, in general, pass through the same point; values of x,y,z deduced from four possible triplets of linear equations will generally differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper forms three surfaces and their linear diameter equations, notes elimination leads to four different possible solutions for intersection coordinates because surface coefficients are independent, and concludes non-coincidence is the general case, while special relations among coefficients produce coincidences. The long omitted 'equation of condition' is referenced; guidance outlines how the condition is derived by elimination and gives the special relations (8) that cause coincidences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem (1): diameters concur when eight points are in special planar positions
rubrics_metrics.description: If all quadrics of second degree passing through the same eight points are cut by planes parallel to a given plane, then the diameters conjugate to these sections all pass through the same point when the eight points lie either in two parallel planes or in the same plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: imposing relations among coefficients (first set of relations (8) in text) yields equal traces on coordinate planes and shows one intersection is a plane curve; elimination and factorization yield that sections are plane curves in parallel planes. Statement (1) summarises this special configuration as a sufficient geometric condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem (2): concurrence when eight points lie on a cylindrical surface
rubrics_metrics.description: If the given plane is parallel to a coordinate plane (e.g., xy), then the diameters conjugate to sections made by planes parallel to this given plane will pass through the same point when the eight common points of the quadrics lie on a cylindrical surface whose generator is parallel to the given plane and whose director is a plane conic of second degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by reducing the equations under assumptions m=n=0 and finding the equation of condition; special relations (10) enforce that the difference of coefficients yields an equation of a cylindrical surface parallel to the chosen plane, thus characterising the necessary geometric configuration for concurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pascal's theorem (A) — new demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: For a hexagon ABCDEF inscribed in a conic, the three points of intersection of opposite sides (AB with DE, BC with EF, CD with FA) are collinear (Pascal line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A coordinate-algebraic proof is given: assign linear equations (1)-(6) to six sides, derive intersection line equations (12)-(14) via elimination and equating coefficients, select multipliers to avoid fractions, and show the resulting line equations for PR and QR coincide, proving collinearity. The exposition emphasises algebraic elimination and multiplier selection as the proof technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brianchon's theorem (B) — new demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: For a hexagon circumscribing a conic, the three diagonals joining opposite vertices (AD, BE, CF) are concurrent (meet at a single point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via dual construction to Pascal: build line equations for diagonals (15)-(17), multiply each by chosen multipliers (N61, M?i, 6i...), add them and use the relations (7,8,9) to show the coefficients vanish so the three diagonal equations are satisfied by the same point, proving concurrence. Emphasises algebraic manipulation and use of earlier elimination relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus of intersections of conjugate tangents of an ellipse
rubrics_metrics.description: The intersections of all conjugate tangents of an ellipse lie on a concentric ellipse whose axes are the diagonals of the squares constructed on the axes of the original ellipse; conjugacy condition given by p1·p2 + ... = 0 (explicit formula in text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition: conjugate tangents are tangents through endpoints of conjugate diameters. Uses tangent equations y= p x + q and conditions for conjugacy (Mathematician vol. i. p.130) to derive relations (4), elimination to obtain the locus equation in x,y which simplifies to an ellipse concentric with the original with computable semi-axes (given formulas). The derivation shows eliminating slope p yields the desired locus and semi-axes.

rubrics_metrics.name: On confocal conic sections: director intersection property
rubrics_metrics.description: If an ellipse and hyperbola share a focus F and intersect in four points A,B,C,D with common director intersection P, then the lines joining paired intersection points (AB, CD, MN, OQ, KL, RS constructed in the paper) all pass through point P (the intersection of directors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic set-up: place focus at origin, write director equations and parametric r expressions for conics; eliminate r to obtain homogeneous second‑degree equations representing straight lines through origin (FA,FB, etc.); evaluate the line equations for AB, CD, etc. and show they are satisfied by the coordinates of P (M=0,T=0), proving concurrency. Also includes corollary about inscribed quadrilaterals whose diagonals pass through a focus producing intersections on the director and bisecting properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of integrals ∫ F(x) log(ax+h) dx when F is rational
rubrics_metrics.description: General method to reduce integrals of the form ∫ F(x) log(ax+h) dx (F rational) to simpler integrals: separate integer part of F, decompose fractional remainder into partial fractions with factors (x−c)^n, integrate terms involving powers with log via integration by parts and derive reduction relations that lower powers (Vm → Vm−1 ...). For quadratic irreducible factors with imaginary roots, combine conjugate terms and express results in logarithms and circular arcs; Spence's logarithmic transcendent L'(x) arises in certain elementary integrals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: write F as integer part + remainder S, expand S as sum of terms of form A/(x−c)^n etc.; integrate terms using repeated integration by parts producing reduction formulae (explicit relation in text) to reduce Vm to lower-order integrals until elementary ones remain. When c is imaginary, combine conjugates to form real integrals expressible via logs and arctangents; when c>0 terms lead to Spence's transcendents L'(x) = ∫ [−log(1−t)/t] dt and related tabulable functions. References to series expansions, change of variables, and methods to reduce integrals to forms suitable for tabulation (Spence's tables) are given.
